| DOM host — elements, text, props, events                      | Included                                                     |
| `Scope`/`defer()`/`acquire()` as component lifecycle          | Included (no new API)                                        |
| `context()` across component boundaries                       | Included (no changes to existing API)                        |
| `RendererProtocol` implemented in DOM host (rAF batching)     | Deferred to v0.3.4                                           |
| Edge cases, error boundaries, polish                          | Deferred to v0.3.4                                           |
| `aljabr/ui/server` SSR host                                   | Deferred — naturally accommodated by `RendererHost` generics |
| `@aljabr/react` adapter                                       | Deferred — contributor decision                              |

## Design Notes

### Components as unions — future consideration

An alternative component model was evaluated during design: components defined as tagged union variants, dispatched via `match()`. Under this model, the component tree is data — serializable, diffable, testable without a DOM.

This was deferred in favor of function components for ergonomic reasons. It is worth revisiting if the function component model shows limitations in practice, or if a data-first component model becomes desirable. Flagged for contributor discussion.

---

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.4): Native UI Layer — Full Implementation

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.3.4.md

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.4): Native UI Layer — Full Implementation

_Minor release following v0.3.3. Completes the `aljabr/ui` layer introduced in v0.3.3: implements the `RendererProtocol` batching escape hatch in the DOM host, hardens edge cases, and polishes the authoring experience._

## Motivation

v0.3.3 ships the core architecture and a working DOM reference implementation. v0.3.4 completes it — the renderer protocol escape hatch, edge cases that surface during real use, and any authoring friction identified after v0.3.3 lands.

## Design Decisions

### `RendererProtocol` — DOM host implementation

The `RendererProtocol` interface was defined in v0.3.3 but not implemented in the DOM host. v0.3.4 wires it up — the DOM host accepts a custom `scheduleFlush` and uses it to batch reactive updates before flushing to the DOM.

Default behavior (no protocol provided) is unchanged: updates flush synchronously. Custom schedulers opt in explicitly:

```ts
// rAF batching — coalesces all updates within a frame into one flush
const { view, mount } = createRenderer(domHost, {
  scheduleFlush(flush) {
    requestAnimationFrame(flush)
  }
})
```

This closes the loop on the `signal` / `signal.protocol` analogy: simple path for most users, escape hatch for performance-sensitive targets.

### Edge cases and hardening

Cases deferred from v0.3.3 that surface during real use:

- Keyed fragment reconciliation — stable identity across conditional swaps
- Nested `ReactiveArray` children — arrays within arrays
- Prop diffing — avoid redundant `setProperty` calls when a reactive prop re-evaluates to the same value
- `null` / `undefined` children — treated as empty, not errors
- Component disposal ordering — LIFO guarantee across nested scopes

### Authoring polish

Any friction identified after v0.3.3 ships. Candidates:

- TypeScript inference for JSX props (narrowing component prop types through `view()`)
- Dev-mode warnings for common mistakes (missing reactive wrapper on dynamic children, unowned signal creation inside `view()`)
- Improved error messages for malformed `ViewNode` structures

## Scope

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| `RendererProtocol` implemented in DOM host | Included |
| rAF batching example / docs | Included |
| Keyed fragment reconciliation | Included |
| Nested `ReactiveArray` children | Included |
| Prop diffing (skip redundant `setProperty`) | Included |
| `null` / `undefined` children | Included |
| Component disposal ordering (LIFO) | Included |
| TypeScript JSX prop inference | Included |
| Dev-mode warnings | Included |
| `aljabr/ui/server` SSR host | To be scoped — depends on demand after v0.3.3 |
| `@aljabr/react` adapter | Contributor decision — revisit after v0.3.3 ships |
| Components as unions (alternative component model) | Contributor discussion — see v0.3.3 design notes |

---

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.5): RefArray Hardening & DerivedArray Rename

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.3.5.md

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.5): RefArray Hardening & DerivedArray Rename

_Patch release following v0.3.4. Addresses type-system gaps and missing array methods surfaced by real-world usage of `RefArray` in application code. Also renames `ReactiveArray` to `DerivedArray` — a hard-break rename with no deprecation alias._

## Motivation

v0.3.4 shipped `RefArray` as the primary reactive array primitive. First-party application code (a todo app built against the published npm package) exposed two classes of issues:

1. **Type coercion gap** — `Ref.create<Task[]>([])` resolves the overload with `T = Task[]`, producing `RefArray<Task[]>` instead of the intended `RefArray<Task>`. The workaround (`Ref.create([] as Task[])`) is non-obvious and easy to miss.
2. **Incomplete method surface** — the mutation and query API is missing methods that authors reach for naturally: `set`, `find`, `findIndex`, `findLastIndex`, `includes`, `join`, `reduce`, `reduceRight`, `shift`, `unshift`.
3. **Confusing dual-array naming** — `ReactiveArray` and `RefArray` share nearly identical query surfaces but have names that don't communicate their relationship or the distinction between mutable source and derived view. Authors reaching for `map`/`filter`/`sort` on a `RefArray` receive a `ReactiveArray` with no clear signal that it is read-only or computed.

This release closes both gaps. It also migrates the destructive read methods (`pop`, `shift`, `Ref.pop`) from `T | undefined` to `Option<T>` — a deliberate breaking change that aligns them with the library's error-handling philosophy.

## Design Decisions

### Type coercion: `Ref.create<T[]>` → `RefArray<T>`

Add a new overload as the first candidate in the overload chain:

```ts
static create<T extends unknown[]>(initial: T): RefArray<T[number]>;
```

When `T = Task[]` is supplied explicitly, `T[number] = Task`, giving `RefArray<Task>`. TypeScript picks this overload first because `T extends unknown[]` is more specific than the existing `T extends object` overloads. The existing overloads and the call-site workaround (`Ref.create([] as Task[])`) remain valid — this is purely additive.

### `set(index, value): Option<T>`

Replace-in-place at a specific index. Fine-grained: dirties only the per-index signal for `index`, leaving all other indices and the length signal untouched.

Out-of-bounds indices return `Option.None` rather than throwing or silently no-opping:

- **No throw** — runtime errors leaking into application code violate the library's design contract.
- **No silent no-op** — invisible failures are harder to debug than explicit ones.
- **`Option<T>` return** — `Some(oldValue)` on success, `None` if the index does not exist. The return type communicates fallibility at authoring time; the author is nudged to handle both branches. The old value is returned as a practical bonus for undo/replace patterns.

```ts
match(tasks.set(idx, updatedTask), {
    Some: (prev) => console.log("replaced", prev),
    None: ()     => console.warn("index gone — reactive update may have changed length"),
});
```

`set` does not extend the array. To append, use `push`; to insert at position, use `splice`.

### Reactive tracked reads: `find`, `findIndex`, `findLastIndex`, `includes`

All four use **precise dependency tracking**: they call `this.get(i)` for each element they visit, registering per-index signal dependencies, and stop at the first match. Elements beyond the match point are not tracked.

Precise tracking is both more efficient and semantically correct:

- An unvisited element can only affect the result if a visited element first changes (stops matching), which triggers a re-run anyway.
- If no visited element changes, the result is guaranteed unchanged regardless of what unvisited elements do.

Return types use `Option` rather than `T | undefined` or `-1` sentinels:

| Method | Return |
|---|---|
| `find(predicate)` | `Option<T>` |
| `findIndex(predicate)` | `Option<number>` |
| `findLastIndex(predicate)` | `Option<number>` |
| `includes(value)` | `boolean` (precise tracking, stops at first match) |

These are synchronous tracked reads — the same pattern as `get(i)` and `length()`. Call them inside `derived()` or `effect()` to register reactive dependencies.

### Reactive tracked reads: `join`, `reduce`, `reduceRight`

Full-array reactive reads: call `this.get(i)` for every index up to `length()`, tracking all per-index signals and the length signal. Any change to any element or the array size triggers re-evaluation.

```ts
derived(() => tasks.join(", "))        // re-runs when any element changes or array grows/shrinks
derived(() => tasks.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.value, 0))
```

Signatures mirror the native `Array` prototype:

```ts
join(separator?: string): string
reduce<U>(fn: (acc: U, item: T, index: number) => U, initial: U): U
reduceRight<U>(fn: (acc: U, item: T, index: number) => U, initial: U): U
```

### Destructive reads: `pop`, `shift`, `Ref.pop` → `Option<T>`

Destructive reads from a possibly-empty container are the clearest case for `Option`: the absence of a value is semantically meaningful, not an error, and callers should be required to handle it.

The following existing and new methods are migrated:

| Method | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| `RefArray.pop()` | `T \| undefined` | `Option<T>` |
| `RefArray.shift()` *(new)* | — | `Option<T>` |
| `Ref.pop(path)` | `ArrayItem<T,P> \| undefined` | `Option<ArrayItem<T,P>>` |

`unshift` remains `void` — it is purely additive and cannot fail.

### `ReactiveArray<T>` → `DerivedArray<T>` (hard-break rename)

`ReactiveArray` is renamed to `DerivedArray`. The name mirrors the existing `Signal`/`Derived` split in the library:

| Mutable | Derived |
|---|---|
| `Signal<T>` | `Derived<T>` |
| `RefArray<T>` | `DerivedArray<T>` |

`DerivedArray` is the type returned by `map`, `filter`, and `sort` on both `RefArray` and `DerivedArray`. It is read-only — it has no mutation methods. Authors cannot construct one directly; it is always the product of a computation over a `RefArray`.

No deprecation alias for `ReactiveArray` is provided. This is a pre-1.0 library and a clean break is preferable to carrying a stale export. Consumers upgrading from v0.3.4 replace `ReactiveArray` with `DerivedArray` at every import and type annotation site — a mechanical find-and-replace.

`IteratorOptions<T>` is unchanged.

### `get()` and `peek()` — whole-value reactive reads

All three array/object containers expose two new no-argument overloads alongside their existing indexed/path signatures:

| Call | Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `RefArray.get()` | `T[]` | Reactive — tracks a root signal notified on every mutation |
| `RefArray.get(i)` | `T \| undefined` | Reactive — tracks the per-index signal (unchanged) |
| `RefArray.peek()` | `T[]` | Untracked snapshot |
| `RefArray.peek(i)` | `T \| undefined` | Untracked snapshot at index |
| `DerivedArray.get()` | `T[]` | Reactive — tracks a dedicated `#rootSignal` fired on every re-computation |
| `DerivedArray.get(i)` | `T \| undefined` | Reactive — per-index signal (unchanged) |
| `DerivedArray.peek()` | `T[]` | Untracked snapshot |
| `DerivedArray.peek(i)` | `T \| undefined` | Untracked snapshot at index |
| `Ref.get()` | `T \| undefined` | Reactive — tracks the root signal at path `""`, notified on any mutation |
| `Ref.get(path)` | `PathValue<T,P> \| undefined` | Reactive — per-path signal (unchanged) |
| `Ref.peek()` | `T \| undefined` | Untracked snapshot |
| `Ref.peek(path)` | `PathValue<T,P> \| undefined` | Untracked snapshot at path |

**Tracking granularity:** `get()` with no arguments is deliberately coarse — it re-runs whenever anything in the container changes. Authors who need fine-grained subscriptions should supply an index/path, or use iterator methods (`filter`, `find`, `reduce`, etc.).

**`DerivedArray` root signal:** `DerivedArray` had no pre-existing root signal (only per-index and length signals). A private `#rootSignal: Signal<T[]>` is added, set in `#applyUpdate` on every re-computation, and disposed alongside the other signals.

**`RefArray` and `Ref` root signal:** Both already had a signal at the array/object root path (`""` for root `Ref`, `prefix` for `RefArray`) that is notified by `applyArrayMutation` and `#notifyRelated` on every write. No new signal is needed — `get()` with no args simply reads that existing signal.

**`peek()` mirrors `get()`:** The overload signatures of `peek()` are identical to `get()` but wrapped in `untrack()`. This matches the convention established by `Signal.peek()`.

### Intentionally retained: `get(i)`, `at(i)`, `Ref.get(path)`

`RefArray.get(i)`, `DerivedArray.get(i)`, and their `at(i)` counterparts remain `T | undefined` and `Derived<T | undefined>` respectively. These are high-frequency reactive read primitives called inside `derived()` and `effect()` on every render cycle, and used internally by `map`, `filter`, `sort`, `find`, `reduce`, and others. Wrapping their return in `Option` would require unwrapping at every internal callsite and add meaningful ceremony to the most common authoring pattern (`tasks.get(0)?.name`).

`Ref.get(path)` is similarly retained: `PathValue<T, P>` is already a deep conditional type, and the `isUnset` property provides a distinct signal for the "no initial value" case.

These are **deliberate holdouts**, not deferred work.

## Scope

| Change | Type |
|---|---|
| `Ref.create<T extends unknown[]>` overload | Type fix |
| `RefArray.set(index, value): Option<T>` | New method |
| `RefArray.find(predicate): Option<T>` | New method |
| `RefArray.findIndex(predicate): Option<number>` | New method |
| `RefArray.findLastIndex(predicate): Option<number>` | New method |
| `RefArray.includes(value): boolean` | New method |
| `RefArray.join(separator?): string` | New method |
| `RefArray.reduce(fn, initial): U` | New method |
| `RefArray.reduceRight(fn, initial): U` | New method |
| `RefArray.shift(): Option<T>` | New method |
| `RefArray.unshift(...items): void` | New method |
| `RefArray.pop(): Option<T>` | **Breaking change** (was `T \| undefined`) |
| `Ref.pop(path): Option<ArrayItem<T,P>>` | **Breaking change** (was `ArrayItem<T,P> \| undefined`) |
| `ReactiveArray<T>` → `DerivedArray<T>` | **Breaking rename** — no deprecation alias |
| `RefArray.get(): T[]` | New overload |
| `RefArray.peek() / peek(i)` | New method |
| `DerivedArray.get(): T[]` | New overload |
| `DerivedArray.peek() / peek(i)` | New method |
| `Ref.get(): T \| undefined` | New overload |
| `Ref.peek() / peek(path)` | New method |

`Signal`, `Derived`, and all schema/ui modules are unchanged.

## Future Work

### `get(i)` / `at(i)` Option ergonomics

The decision to keep `get(i): T | undefined` is load-bearing for authoring ergonomics today. If a future version introduces a more concise unwrap idiom (e.g. a pipeline operator or a dedicated `Option.from(nullable)` bridge), revisiting these as `Option<T>` becomes more attractive. Revisit before v0.4.0.

---

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.7): Iterator Reactivity & List Reconciliation

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.3.7.md

# Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.7): Iterator Reactivity & List Reconciliation

_Patch release following v0.3.6. Completes the reactive list reconciliation work deferred since v0.3.4: per-index scopes in the renderer, keyed DOM reconciliation, and key propagation through all six iterator methods that produce a `DerivedArray`. Also fixes the local dev environment._

## Motivation

Since v0.3.4, `mountDerivedArray` in the renderer has carried a documented deferral:

```
// Fine-grained per-index updates are left for v0.3.4.
```

The consequence is visible in real application code: any mutation to a reactive list — toggle, add, remove, filter change — tears down and re-mounts the **entire** rendered list. Every item re-renders on every change, regardless of whether its data changed.

This release closes that gap completely. The fix spans two layers: the `DerivedArray` data model (key propagation through the iterator chain) and the renderer (per-index scopes, then keyed reconciliation). All six methods that produce a `DerivedArray` are addressed — none are left behind.

## Design Decisions

### Key propagation through the iterator chain

`DerivedArray` and `RefArray` each expose three iterator methods that return a new `DerivedArray`: `map`, `filter`, and `sort`. Key information must survive the entire chain for the renderer to reconcile lists surgically. The current state of each method:

| Method | Source | Current key handling | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RefArray.map()` | mutable root | `keyFn = null`, no `opts` | No way to inject a key |
| `RefArray.filter()` | mutable root | `opts?.key ?? identity` | None — root source, nothing to inherit |
| `RefArray.sort()` | mutable root | `opts?.key ?? identity` | None — root source, nothing to inherit |
| `DerivedArray.map()` | derived | `keyFn = null` | Source key silently dropped |
| `DerivedArray.filter()` | derived | `opts?.key ?? identity` | Falls back to identity when source has a key |
| `DerivedArray.sort()` | derived | `opts?.key ?? identity` | Falls back to identity when source has a key |

**`DerivedArray.filter()` and `DerivedArray.sort()` — inherit source key**

When no `opts.key` is provided and the source `DerivedArray` already has a `#keyFn`, inherit it instead of defaulting to reference identity. The items produced by filter and sort are a subset or reorder of the source items, so the source key function is valid for them.

```ts
// before — key lost on chained filter
const done = visibleTasks.filter(t => isDone(t));        // keyFn = identity (wrong)

// after — key inherited from visibleTasks
const done = visibleTasks.filter(t => isDone(t));        // keyFn = taskId (inherited)
```

`keyIsDefault` is cleared when a key is inherited this way — no warning is emitted.

**`DerivedArray.map()` — index-based key inheritance**

`map` changes the element type (`T → U`), so the source key function cannot operate on the mapped items directly. Instead, `map` inherits the source key as an index-based lookup: a closure over the source array that resolves `sourceKeyFn(source.peek(i))` for index `i`. The resulting `DerivedArray<U>` carries this index key and exposes it via `keyAt(i)`.

```ts
// key is taskId on visibleTasks; rows inherits it index-by-index
const rows = visibleTasks.map(task => <TaskItem task={task} />);
rows.keyAt(0); // → taskId(visibleTasks.peek(0))
```

**`RefArray.map()` — add `opts` parameter**

`RefArray` is the mutable root; it has no key to inherit. Authors mapping directly off a `RefArray` (without a prior `filter` or `sort` step) have no current way to inject a key. Add `opts?: { key: (item: T) => unknown }` to `RefArray.map()` to close this gap.

```ts
const rows = tasks.map(task => <TaskItem task={task} />, { key: taskId });
```

**`keyAt(i): unknown | null` — public key surface on `DerivedArray`**

Add a single public method that the renderer uses to retrieve the key for any index. Implementation:

- For `filter`/`sort` arrays: `#keyFn(#items[i])`.
- For `map` arrays with an inherited source key: delegates to the stored index-based closure.
- For `map` arrays with no key (e.g. mapping off an unkeyed `RefArray`): returns `null`.

`null` signals the renderer to fall back to position-based reconciliation for that array.

### Renderer — Phase A: per-index scopes (position-based)

Replace the current `mountDerivedArray` implementation, which subscribes to all signals in a single `effectOwner` and tears down the entire list on any change, with per-index owner scopes.

Each index `i` gets its own `Computation` that subscribes only to `arr.get(i)`. The outer `effectOwner` subscribes only to `arr.length()`:

- **Length increases**: create new per-index scopes for the appended indices.
- **Length decreases**: dispose trailing scopes; their cleanups remove the corresponding DOM nodes.
- **`arr.get(i)` changes**: only the scope at index `i` re-runs, reconciling the old `Child` at that position with the new one.

This eliminates full-list re-renders for the common cases: in-place mutation (toggle), append (add), and tail removal (remove last).

### Renderer — Phase B: keyed scopes

Per-index scopes (Phase A) handle structural changes by position. When items are reordered or removed from the middle of a filtered list, items shift positions: their per-index signals fire and they re-render even though their data is unchanged.

Keyed scopes bind the scope's lifetime to item identity rather than position.

The renderer checks `arr.keyAt(i)` on the first render and after each length change to determine whether to use keyed or position-based mode:

- If `keyAt` returns non-null values: **keyed mode**.
- If `keyAt` returns null: **position-based mode** (Phase A).

**Keyed mode implementation:**

Maintain `Map<unknown, { scope: Computation; start: N; end: N }>` — one entry per live item, keyed by the value returned from `keyAt`.

On each update (triggered by the length signal or root signal):

1. Compute old key list and new key list.
2. **Removed keys**: dispose the scope; remove all DOM nodes between its `start` and `end` anchors.
3. **New keys**: create a fresh scope; insert its `start`/`end` anchors and reconcile the item at the correct position.
4. **Moved keys** (same key, new position): re-insert the existing `start`/`end` anchors and all nodes between them at the new position in the DOM — without disposing or re-running the scope.
5. **Same key, changed value** (`keyAt(i)` unchanged but `arr.get(i)` reference changed): the per-index signal fires and the scope re-runs at its current position.

The result: a task toggled from Active to Done re-renders only its own row. A filter change that removes one item from the middle of the list moves the remaining items' DOM nodes without re-rendering them.

### Dev environment

`public/index.html` references `./main.tsx` but the file is named `maint.tsx` (typo). Rename `public/maint.tsx` → `public/main.tsx`. No config changes required — Vite's dev server (`npm run dev`) already serves `public/` correctly once the filename matches.

## Scope

| Change | Type |
|---|---|
| `DerivedArray.filter()`: inherit source `#keyFn` when no `opts.key` provided | Fix |
| `DerivedArray.sort()`: inherit source `#keyFn` when no `opts.key` provided | Fix |
| `DerivedArray.map()`: propagate source key via index-based closure | Fix |
| `RefArray.map()`: add `opts?: { key: (item: T) => unknown }` | Enhancement |
| `DerivedArray.keyAt(i): unknown \| null` | New method |
| `mountDerivedArray`: per-index owner scopes (Phase A) | Fix |
| `mountDerivedArray`: keyed scope reconciliation (Phase B) | Fix |
| `public/maint.tsx` → `public/main.tsx` | Fix |

## Future Work

### Keyed portal / cross-renderer composition

Keyed reconciliation within a single renderer is complete after this release. Composition across renderers (e.g. a DOM list item that contains a canvas sub-renderer) is a userland pattern today — spawn a new renderer root, tie its cleanup to the parent owner. If the pattern proves common in application code, a first-class `createPortal` primitive will be considered for `aljabr/ui` in a future version.

---

# v0.3.8.md

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.3.8.md

### **Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.8): Canvas Renderer**

**Strategic Vision**

With the reactive primitive layer (`aljabr/prelude`, `aljabr/signals`) and the DOM renderer (`aljabr/ui/dom`) shipping in prior versions, v0.3.8 introduces a first-class canvas renderer at `aljabr/ui/canvas`. The goal is a fully pluggable, retained-mode canvas host that implements the existing `RendererHost<N, E>` contract — requiring zero changes to the core reconciler — and ships alongside a JSX namespace, a `Viewport` factory for pan/zoom, and an inherited paint property system via the context API.

The canvas renderer is a pure library export with no external dependencies. Authors building diagramming tools, data visualization plugins, or canvas-based UIs get a reactive, JSX-driven scene graph that integrates naturally with the rest of the Aljabr reactive stack. The diagramming plugin that motivated this work is an application-layer concern; the renderer itself stays general-purpose.

### **Table of Contents**

- **1.0 Phase 1: Module Scaffolding & JSX Rename**
    - _Focus: Establishing the new module structure, moving DOM JSX to its symmetric location, and wiring up the build pipeline._
- **2.0 Phase 2: Canvas Node Model & Host Skeleton**
    - _Focus: Defining `CanvasNode` as an aljabr union (parallel to `ViewNode`) and implementing the `RendererHost<CanvasNode, CanvasElementNode>` interface skeleton._
- **3.0 Phase 3: Paint Pass & Primitive Rendering**
    - _Focus: Implementing the full paint loop — all geometric primitives, group transforms, zIndex sorting, and full-canvas clear + repaint._
- **4.0 Phase 4: Viewport, Culling & rAF Batching**
    - _Focus: `Viewport` factory, `RendererProtocol` wired to `requestAnimationFrame`, and viewport-bounds culling to keep large graphs performant._
- **5.0 Phase 5: Inherited Paint Props & Text Layout**
    - _Focus: Context-based font/color inheritance, text layout props (`textAlign`, `verticalAlign`, `padding`), and implicit string-child wrapping._
- **6.0 Phase 6: Hit Testing & Event Dispatch**
    - _Focus: Bounding-box hit testing, scene-graph event bubbling, `on*` prop dispatch, and pixel-perfect opt-in._
- **7.0 Phase 7: Export Surface & Canvas JSX Runtime**
    - _Focus: Full `JSX.IntrinsicElements` namespace for canvas primitives, final export surface, and package.json wiring._

### Phase 1: Module Scaffolding & JSX Rename

_Establish the correct module hierarchy before any canvas code lands. The DOM JSX runtime currently lives at the wrong address (`aljabr/ui/jsx-runtime`); the canvas work is the right moment to fix it._

#### 1.1 — DOM JSX Rename

Move `src/ui/jsx-runtime.ts` and `src/ui/jsx-dev-runtime.ts` into `src/ui/dom/`:

```
src/ui/dom/jsx-runtime.ts      (was: src/ui/jsx-runtime.ts)
src/ui/dom/jsx-dev-runtime.ts  (was: src/ui/jsx-dev-runtime.ts)
```

Update all imports within the codebase accordingly. No re-export shim is needed — this is a pre-alpha library with no production consumers.

Update `package.json` exports:

```json
"./ui/dom/jsx-runtime":     { ... },
"./ui/dom/jsx-dev-runtime": { ... }
```

Remove the old `"./ui/jsx-runtime"` and `"./ui/jsx-dev-runtime"` entries entirely.

Update `vite.config.ts` to rename the entry keys:

- `ui-jsx-runtime` → `ui-dom-jsx-runtime`
- `ui-jsx-dev-runtime` → `ui-dom-jsx-dev-runtime`

#### 1.2 — Canvas Module Skeleton

Create the following empty files (stubs to be filled in later phases):

```
src/ui/canvas/host.ts          — RendererHost implementation
src/ui/canvas/index.ts         — module exports
src/ui/canvas/jsx-runtime.ts   — canvas JSX factory + IntrinsicElements
src/ui/canvas/jsx-dev-runtime.ts
```

Add `package.json` exports:

```json
"./ui/canvas": {
    "import": "./dist/ui-canvas.js",
    "require": "./dist/ui-canvas.cjs",
    "types": "./dist/ui/canvas/index.d.ts"
},
"./ui/canvas/jsx-runtime": {
    "import": "./dist/ui-canvas-jsx-runtime.js",
    "require": "./dist/ui-canvas-jsx-runtime.cjs",
    "types": "./dist/ui/canvas/jsx-runtime.d.ts"
},
"./ui/canvas/jsx-dev-runtime": {
    "import": "./dist/ui-canvas-jsx-dev-runtime.js",
    "require": "./dist/ui-canvas-jsx-dev-runtime.cjs",
    "types": "./dist/ui/canvas/jsx-dev-runtime.d.ts"
}
```

Add corresponding entry points in `vite.config.ts`:

- `ui-canvas` → `src/ui/canvas/index.ts`
- `ui-canvas-jsx-runtime` → `src/ui/canvas/jsx-runtime.ts`
- `ui-canvas-jsx-dev-runtime` → `src/ui/canvas/jsx-dev-runtime.ts`

### Phase 2: Canvas Node Model & Host Skeleton

_Define `CanvasNode` as an aljabr union — parallel to `ViewNode` — and implement the `RendererHost<CanvasNode, CanvasElementNode>` interface._

#### 2.1 — `CanvasNode` as an Aljabr Union

`CanvasNode` follows the same pattern as `ViewNode`: named `Variant<>` types per variant, an internal `union()` factory, and a typed façade constant that shares the type name.

```ts
// src/ui/canvas/node.ts

import { union, type Variant } from "aljabr";

export type CanvasTag =
    | "rect"
    | "circle"
    | "ellipse"
    | "line"
    | "path"
    | "group"
    | "text";

export interface CanvasBounds {
    x: number;
    y: number;
    width: number;
    height: number;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Variant payload types
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

export type CanvasElementNode = Variant<
    "Element",
    {
        tag: CanvasTag;
        props: Record<string, unknown>;
        children: CanvasNode[];
        parent: CanvasElementNode | null;
        bounds: CanvasBounds; // eager — recomputed on geometry prop change
        zIndex: number; // defaults to 0
        hitTest?: (x: number, y: number) => boolean; // pixel-perfect opt-in
    }
>;

export type CanvasTextNode = Variant<"Text", { content: string }>;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// CanvasNode — the union type
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

export type CanvasNode = CanvasElementNode | CanvasTextNode;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Internal factory
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

const _canvasFactory = union({
    Element: (p: {
        tag: CanvasTag;
        props: Record<string, unknown>;
        children: any[];
        parent: CanvasElementNode | null;
        bounds: CanvasBounds;
        zIndex: number;
        hitTest?: (x: number, y: number) => boolean;
    }) => p,
    Text: (content: string) => ({ content }),
});

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// CanvasNode — typed façade (value and type share the name)
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

export const CanvasNode = _canvasFactory as unknown as {
    Element(p: {
        tag: CanvasTag;
        props: Record<string, unknown>;
        children: CanvasNode[];
        parent: CanvasElementNode | null;
        bounds: CanvasBounds;
        zIndex: number;
        hitTest?: (x: number, y: number) => boolean;
    }): CanvasElementNode;
    Text(content: string): CanvasTextNode;
};
```

`CanvasBounds` is recomputed eagerly in `setProperty` whenever a geometry prop changes (`x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `r`, `rx`, `ry`, `x1`, `y1`, `x2`, `y2`). For `path` elements, bounds are derived from the path bounding box via a lightweight parser. For `group` elements, bounds are the union of all descendant bounds — computed lazily and invalidated when any descendant geometry prop changes.

Because `CanvasNode` is an aljabr union, the reconciler and paint pass can use `match` to dispatch on variant — the same exhaustive pattern matching used throughout the rest of the library.

#### 2.2 — `RendererHost<CanvasNode, CanvasElementNode>` Implementation

The host is typed as `RendererHost<CanvasNode, CanvasElementNode>` — `CanvasElementNode` (not the full union) is the `E` parameter, mirroring how the DOM host is `RendererHost<Node, Element>`.

Implement all required host methods:

| Method                           | Canvas behaviour                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `createElement(tag)`             | Returns `CanvasNode.Element({ tag, props: {}, children: [], parent: null, bounds: zeroBounds(), zIndex: 0 })`           |
| `createText(text)`               | Returns `CanvasNode.Text(text)`                                                                                         |
| `insert(parent, child, anchor?)` | Appends `child` to `parent.children` before `anchor` if provided, otherwise at end                                      |
| `remove(child)`                  | Removes `child` from its parent's `children`; sets `child.parent` to `null` for `Element` nodes                         |
| `setProperty(el, key, value)`    | Assigns to `el.props[key]`; recomputes `el.bounds` if a geometry key changed; updates `el.zIndex` if `key === "zIndex"` |
| `setText(node, text)`            | Matched via `match(node, { Text: (n) => n.content = text, Element: () => {} })`                                         |
| `parentNode(node)`               | `match(node, { Element: (n) => n.parent, Text: () => null })`                                                           |
| `nextSibling(node)`              | Walks `parent.children` to find the node after this one                                                                 |

`onMount`, `onUnmount`, `onUpdate` are not implemented in Phase 2 — canvas elements have no meaningful lifecycle hooks at the host level.

### Phase 3: Paint Pass & Primitive Rendering

_Implement the full repaint loop: clear the canvas, walk the scene graph, paint each primitive._

#### 3.1 — Paint Loop

The paint function is called by the `RendererProtocol` flush (Phase 4). It receives the `CanvasElementNode` root and a `CanvasRenderingContext2D`. Dispatch is via `match` on the `CanvasNode` union:

```
paintNode(ctx, node):
    match(node, {
        Text: () => return,              (bare text handled by parent's implicit wrap)
        Element: (el) =>
            ctx.save()
            applyTransform(ctx, el.props)    (x, y, scale, rotate for group)
            sortChildrenByZIndex(el.children)
            paintShape(ctx, el)
            for child of el.children:
                paintNode(ctx, child)
            ctx.restore()
    })
```

Children are sorted by `zIndex` in place during the paint pass. Insertion order is the tiebreaker for equal `zIndex` values.

#### 3.2 — Primitive Paint Implementations

Each `CanvasTag` maps to a set of `ctx` calls:

| Tag       | Canvas calls                                         | Key props                                                                                        |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `rect`    | `ctx.fillRect` / `ctx.strokeRect` or `ctx.roundRect` | `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `rx`, `fill`, `stroke`, `strokeWidth`                               |
| `circle`  | `ctx.arc` (full circle)                              | `cx`, `cy`, `r`, `fill`, `stroke`, `strokeWidth`                                                 |
| `ellipse` | `ctx.ellipse`                                        | `cx`, `cy`, `rx`, `ry`, `fill`, `stroke`, `strokeWidth`                                          |
| `line`    | `ctx.moveTo` + `ctx.lineTo`                          | `x1`, `y1`, `x2`, `y2`, `stroke`, `strokeWidth`, `lineCap`                                       |
| `path`    | `ctx.Path2D`                                         | `d` (SVG path string), `fill`, `stroke`, `strokeWidth`                                           |
| `group`   | transform only — no shape paint                      | `x`, `y`, `scale`, `rotate`                                                                      |
| `text`    | `ctx.fillText`                                       | `x`, `y`, `content`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `fill`, `textAlign`, `textBaseline` |

Fill and stroke semantics follow SVG conventions: `fill="none"` skips fill; `stroke="none"` skips stroke. Both default to `none` unless set.

#### 3.3 — Group Transforms

`applyTransform` applies structured transform props to the canvas context before painting children:

```ts
ctx.translate(x ?? 0, y ?? 0);
ctx.rotate(((rotate ?? 0) * Math.PI) / 180);
ctx.scale(scale ?? 1, scale ?? 1);
```

All transforms are relative — they compose with the parent's accumulated transform via `ctx.save()` / `ctx.restore()`. There is no matrix prop; authors compose transforms by nesting `<group>` elements.

### Phase 4: Viewport, Culling & rAF Batching

_Wire up the `RendererProtocol` to `requestAnimationFrame`, implement the `Viewport` factory, and skip painting off-screen nodes._

#### 4.1 — rAF Protocol

```ts
const rafProtocol: RendererProtocol = {
    scheduleFlush(flush) {
        requestAnimationFrame(flush);
    },
};
```

#### 4.2 — `createCanvasRenderer`

A convenience wrapper that pre-wires `canvasHost` with `rafProtocol`:

```ts
export function createCanvasRenderer(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d")!;
    const { view, mount } = createRenderer(canvasHost, rafProtocol);
    return {
        view,
        mount: (component: () => ViewNode) => {
            const unmount = mount(component, createRootElement(canvas, ctx));
            return unmount;
        },
    };
}
```

`createRootElement` allocates a synthetic root `CanvasElementNode` (via `CanvasNode.Element(...)`) that holds a reference to `ctx` and the canvas dimensions. The paint loop reads `ctx` and dimensions from this root.

#### 4.3 — `Viewport` Factory

`Viewport` is a factory (not a hook — consistent with the `Scope` naming convention) that owns pan/zoom state as signals and exposes the viewport bounds needed for culling:

```ts
interface ViewportHandle {
    x: Signal<number>;
    y: Signal<number>;
    scale: Signal<number>;
    bounds(): CanvasBounds; // derived — current visible world-space rect
    reset(): void;
}

export function Viewport(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement): ViewportHandle;
```

The `bounds()` derived is what the paint loop uses for culling. Authors feed `x`, `y`, `scale` into a root `<group>` as reactive props:

```tsx
const vp = Viewport(canvasEl);

<group x={vp.x} y={vp.y} scale={vp.scale}>
    {/* all diagram content */}
</group>;
```

#### 4.4 — Viewport Culling

Before painting each `CanvasElementNode`, the paint loop intersects `node.bounds` with the current viewport world-space bounds. If there is no intersection the node and its entire subtree are skipped:

```
intersects(node.bounds, viewport.bounds()) → false: skip
```

Bounds are in world space (pre-transform). For `group` elements the bounds are the union of all descendant bounds — computed lazily, cached, invalidated when any descendant geometry prop changes.

### Phase 5: Inherited Paint Props & Text Layout

_Implement context-based inheritance for font and color props, text layout positioning, and implicit string-child wrapping._

#### 5.1 — Inherited Paint Props via Context

Font and color props propagate down the scene graph using the existing `context()` API from `aljabr/signals`. A `PaintContext` holds the current inherited values and is provided at each `<group>` that sets any of these props:

Inheritable props:

| Prop          | Default        |
| ------------- | -------------- |
| `fontFamily`  | `"sans-serif"` |
| `fontSize`    | `14`           |
| `fontWeight`  | `"normal"`     |
| `fill`        | `"none"`       |
| `stroke`      | `"none"`       |
| `strokeWidth` | `1`            |

During the paint pass, each node reads the resolved value for a prop by checking `node.props[key]` first, falling back to the inherited context value. The context is updated at `group` boundaries when the group's props override any inheritable key.

#### 5.2 — Text Layout Props

The following props control how an implicit or explicit `<text>` child is positioned within a parent element's bounds. They are also inheritable via context:

| Prop            | Values                                               | Default  |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `textAlign`     | `"left"` \| `"center"` \| `"right"`                  | `"left"` |
| `verticalAlign` | `"top"` \| `"middle"` \| `"bottom"`                  | `"top"`  |
| `padding`       | `number` (uniform) or `{ top, right, bottom, left }` | `0`      |

When a `<text>` element is rendered as a child of a shape element, its `x` and `y` are computed from the parent's bounds + layout props rather than taken from its own props:

```
contentX:
    "left"   → parent.bounds.x + padding.left
    "center" → parent.bounds.x + parent.bounds.width / 2
    "right"  → parent.bounds.x + parent.bounds.width - padding.right

contentY:
    "top"    → parent.bounds.y + padding.top + fontSize (baseline offset)
    "middle" → parent.bounds.y + parent.bounds.height / 2
    "bottom" → parent.bounds.y + parent.bounds.height - padding.bottom

ctx.textAlign    = textAlign
ctx.textBaseline = "middle" for verticalAlign "middle", else "alphabetic"
```

#### 5.3 — Implicit Text Wrapping

When the reconciler encounters a `CanvasTextNode` (a `CanvasNode.Text(...)` variant) as a direct child of a non-`text` `CanvasElementNode`, the canvas host's `insert()` method automatically wraps it in a synthetic `CanvasNode.Element({ tag: "text", ... })` inheriting the parent's layout context. The synthetic element is internal — it does not appear in the scene graph as an authored node, only as a render-time detail.

In dev mode, the host warns if a `CanvasTextNode` is inserted into a `path` or `line` element (which have no meaningful bounding box for layout).

Word wrapping is explicitly out of scope. Authors requiring multi-line text should implement wrapping as a component that emits multiple `<text>` elements, or integrate an external library (e.g. Pretext).

### Phase 6: Hit Testing & Event Dispatch

_Implement pointer event handling: bounding-box hit tests, scene-graph bubbling, and the `on*` prop dispatch convention._

#### 6.1 — Event Listener Setup

`createCanvasRenderer` attaches a single set of pointer event listeners to the `<canvas>` DOM element during mount:

```
pointerdown, pointerup, pointermove, pointerenter, pointerleave, click, dblclick, contextmenu, wheel
```

Each listener extracts `(offsetX, offsetY)` from the native event (already in canvas coordinate space) and initiates a hit test against the scene graph.

#### 6.2 — Bounding-Box Hit Test

The hit test walks the scene graph in **reverse paint order** (last painted = topmost = checked first). `CanvasTextNode` variants are skipped — only `CanvasElementNode` variants participate in hit testing. For each `CanvasElementNode`:

1. Check `node.bounds` contains `(x, y)` in world space (apply accumulated inverse transforms)
2. If the node has a `hitTest` function, call it for pixel-perfect verification
3. First node that passes is the hit target

Groups are transparent to hit testing — a pointer event passes through a group to its children, and bubbles back up through the group after the deepest hit is found.

#### 6.3 — Event Bubbling

Starting from the deepest hit node, dispatch the event upward through `parent` pointers until the root is reached or a handler calls `event.stopPropagation()`. Each node's `on*` prop matching the event type is called:

```
onPointerDown → "pointerdown"
onClick       → "click"
onWheel       → "wheel"
... etc.
```

The synthetic canvas event passed to handlers mirrors the native `PointerEvent` interface with an additional `target: CanvasElementNode` field. `stopPropagation()` halts the bubble; `preventDefault()` is forwarded to the native event.

#### 6.4 — Pixel-Perfect Opt-In

Authors can attach a hit-test override on any element for irregular shapes. The prop is named **`onHitTest`** (not `hitTest`) so the reconciler's existing `on*` rule routes it through as a non-reactive callback — without the `on` prefix, the reconciler would invoke the function as a reactive getter and store its result on the element instead. The host then hoists `onHitTest` onto the variant payload's `hitTest` field; the hit walker reads it from there.

```tsx
<path d={arcPath} onHitTest={(x, y) => ctx.isPointInPath(path2D, x, y)} />
```

The offscreen canvas approach (unique-color rendering per node) is an alternative implementation strategy for the override — authors may use it, but the renderer does not provide it as a built-in. The contract is simply `(x: number, y: number) => boolean`, called with the element's local-frame coordinates after the inverse transform walk.

### Phase 7: Export Surface & Canvas JSX Runtime

_Finalize the public API: the canvas JSX namespace, the export surface of `aljabr/ui/canvas`, and end-to-end integration testing._

#### 7.1 — Canvas JSX Runtime

`src/ui/canvas/jsx-runtime.ts` exports `jsx`, `jsxs`, and the `JSX` namespace. The factory is identical to the DOM version (`_jsx` → `view()`). The namespace declares canvas-specific intrinsic elements:

```ts
declare namespace JSX {
    interface IntrinsicElements {
        rect: RectProps;
        circle: CircleProps;
        ellipse: EllipseProps;
        line: LineProps;
        path: PathProps;
        group: GroupProps;
        text: TextProps;
    }
}
```

Each props interface is typed with both geometry props and the full set of inheritable paint props (`fill`, `stroke`, `fontFamily`, etc.) as optional keys. `on*` event handlers accept `(event: CanvasSyntheticEvent) => void`.

Authors set `jsxImportSource: "aljabr/ui/canvas"` in their `tsconfig.json` (or use a per-file `/** @jsxImportSource aljabr/ui/canvas */` pragma) for canvas component files. DOM and canvas component files use separate `jsxImportSource` values — the boundary type at interop points is `ViewNode`, which both runtimes produce.

#### 7.2 — Export Surface of `aljabr/ui/canvas`

`src/ui/canvas/index.ts` exports:

```ts
export { canvasHost }; // RendererHost<CanvasNode, CanvasElementNode>
export { createCanvasRenderer }; // pre-wired with rAF protocol
export { Viewport }; // pan/zoom factory
export { zeroBounds }; // CanvasBounds zero-rect helper
export type {
    CanvasNode,
    CanvasElementNode,
    CanvasTextNode,
    CanvasBounds,
    CanvasTag,
};
export type { ViewportHandle };
```

The `CanvasNode` *value* (the variant factory used as `CanvasNode.Element({...})` / `CanvasNode.Text("…")`) is not re-exported from this barrel — `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` rejects exporting the same identifier as both a type and a value through this surface. Authors who need the factory import it directly from `aljabr/ui/canvas/node`. In practice this is rare: `canvasHost.createElement` / `createText` plus the JSX runtime cover all normal construction sites.

Not exported: internal paint utilities, the rAF protocol object (authors who need a custom protocol use `createRenderer(canvasHost, myProtocol)` directly from `aljabr/ui`).

#### 7.3 — Implementation Order

1. Phase 1: module scaffolding + DOM JSX rename
2. Phase 2: type definitions + host skeleton (all methods stubbed with no-ops)
3. Phase 3: paint loop + all primitive renderers
4. Phase 4: rAF protocol + `Viewport` + viewport culling
5. Phase 5: paint prop inheritance + text layout + implicit wrapping
6. Phase 6: hit testing + event bubbling + `on*` dispatch
7. Phase 7: JSX runtime + export surface + integration tests

Tests live in `test/ui/canvas/`, one file per phase concern. Each phase ships with tests before the next begins.

### Design Constraints

- **Zero external dependencies.** The canvas renderer uses only the browser Canvas API and existing `aljabr` internals.
- **No layout engine.** Single-line text layout only. Word wrap is an application concern.
- **No word wrap.** Authors integrate external libraries (e.g. Pretext) as needed.
- **Renderer-agnostic `ViewNode`.** The canvas renderer produces and consumes the same `ViewNode` / `Child` types as the DOM renderer. No new core types.
- **`createPortal` is not part of this release.** Portal-style cross-renderer composition is a userland pattern (spawn a new renderer root, tie its cleanup to the parent owner). If the pattern proves sound in application code, it will be promoted to `aljabr/ui` in a future version.

### Additional Minor Fixes

- **`Option.toResult` async-error overload + `Result.Expect<T, E>` rejection-type tracking.** Adds a third `Option.toResult` overload accepting an async error thunk (`() => Promise<E>`), which lifts `None` into a `Result.Expect` whose pending promise rejects with the constructed `E`. To make this honest, `Expected` gains a phantom `E` parameter (`Expected<T, E = never>`), `Thenable.then` defaults `TResult2 = E` so rejection type propagates through chains, `onRejected`'s `reason` narrows from `any` to `E`, and a `Thenable.catch` shorthand is added. Also fixes an overload-ordering bug in the existing `toResult` thunk path (sync thunks were inferring `E = () => string` instead of `E = string`).

---

# v0.3.9.md

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.3.9.md

### **Aljabr Roadmap (v0.3.9): Canvas Bounds Completeness**

**Strategic Vision**

v0.3.8 shipped a canvas renderer with three deliberate bounds deferrals — `<path>`, `<group>`, and `<text>` all return `zeroBounds()` from the host's `recomputeBounds` switch. The paint pass and hit-test walker compensate via the `hasCullableBounds(b) ⇒ b.width > 0 && b.height > 0` rule and the `onHitTest`-is-authoritative escape hatch from §6.4: zero-area bounds always paint (no culling) and only-the-override-decides-the-hit. That tradeoff is functionally correct but optimisation-visible — large scenes pay per-child intersect tests instead of group-level skips, and pixel-perfect hit testing must be hand-rolled by the author for every path or label they want clickable.

v0.3.9 lifts those three deferrals so every primitive carries meaningful bounds. Once each tag grows real bounds, the existing `intersects()` / `boundsContains()` checks engage automatically — there are no new code paths in `paint.ts` or `hit-test.ts`. This is a tightly-scoped completeness release; no new user-facing features.

The renderer's external surface (`aljabr/ui/canvas/index.ts`) does not change. Only `host.ts`'s `recomputeBounds` and the per-primitive bounds modules grow code.

### **Table of Contents**

- **1.0 Phase 1: Path Bounds**
    - _Focus: derive a bounding box from an SVG path string at `setProperty("d", …)` time so paths participate in viewport culling and bounds-driven hit testing._
- **2.0 Phase 2: Group Bounds (Descendant Union)**
    - _Focus: lazy, dirty-bit-driven recompute of a group's bounds as the union of its descendants, invalidated by any geometry change in the subtree._
- **3.0 Phase 3: Text Bounds**
    - _Focus: measure rendered text width/height via a shared offscreen canvas so text elements cull correctly and bounds-only hit testing matches the painted glyphs._
- **4.0 Out of Scope (Tracked)**
    - _Items that surfaced during the v0.3.8 implementation but are intentionally not part of v0.3.9._

### Phase 1: Path Bounds

#### 1.1 — The Deferral

`src/ui/canvas/host.ts`'s `recomputeBounds` returns `zeroBounds()` for `<path>` elements:

```ts
when({ tag: "path" }, () => zeroBounds()),
```

Consequences in production code:

- **Culling**: `paint.ts`'s `hasCullableBounds` short-circuits paths to "always paint" — viewport culling never trims a path subtree even when it's miles off-screen.
- **Hit testing**: `hit-test.ts`'s `hitTestNode` only finds a path when the author provides an `onHitTest` override (Phase 7's authoritative-override fix). A bare `<path d="…">` is unhittable by bounds alone.

The `<path>` integration test in `test/ui/canvas/integration.test.ts` exists exactly because of this gap — it pins the override-path semantics so the gap can be lifted without regression.

#### 1.2 — Motivations for Deferral

SVG path strings carry the full grammar: `M`, `L`, `H`, `V`, `C`, `S`, `Q`, `T`, `A`, `Z`, plus their relative-coordinate lowercase variants. A *correct* bounding box requires evaluating bezier extrema — for a cubic curve, the bounds aren't `(min(p0, p1, p2, p3), max(...))` because the curve can swing outside its control points along the parameter `t`. The exact extrema solve `B'(t) = 0`, a small derivative-root problem per axis.

Phase 2 of v0.3.8 was structured around the union shape and the host skeleton — landing a path-string parser at that point would have doubled the file's surface area for a feature the rest of v0.3.8 didn't strictly need (every other primitive computes its bounds from numeric props directly). The roadmap `§2.1` explicitly noted "For `path` elements, bounds are derived from the path bounding box via a lightweight parser" as a follow-on item, and the comment in `recomputeBounds` was kept honest: "Path (SVG path-string parsing) and group (union of descendants) bounds remain deferred."

#### 1.3 — Implementation Strategy Options

| Option | Approach | Approx. LOC | Correctness | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **Endpoint-only union** — parse only `M`/`L`/`H`/`V`/`Z` start/end points; treat curves as straight lines. | ~30 | Under-paints curves (curve arcs may extend outside the endpoint hull). | Cheapest; only correct for poly-line paths. **Rejected** — under-painting silently hides geometry, which is the one failure mode we should never ship. |
| 2 | **Control-point hull** — parse all command operands (including bezier / quadratic control points and arc box corners), take min/max of every reference point. | ~50 | Always correct; can overestimate by the curve's hull-vs-curve gap. | Good balance: never under-paints, modest code, no math beyond min/max. Same model as SVG's own bounding-box recommendations for editors that want a fast-path. |
| 3 | **Bezier extrema** — solve `B'(t) = 0` per axis to find tight bounds for each curve segment. | ~150 | Tight bounds. | More math, more allocation per geometry change. Worth it if a future profile shows the hull's overestimate is the bottleneck. |
| 4 | **`Path2D` + `OffscreenCanvas` rasterisation** — construct `new Path2D(d)`, render to a 1×1 offscreen canvas, query the resulting transform extent. | ~40 | Tight bounds via the browser's own rasteriser. | Browser-only (no Node fallback for any future SSR experiments); brittle if Path2D bounding semantics shift; needs an offscreen canvas allocation per measurement. |

**Recommendation: Option 2 (control-point hull).** Best balance of correctness, code size, and zero external dependencies. The overestimate is bounded by the curve's hull, which for typical diagramming paths (rounded corners, gentle bezier connectors) is well within an order of magnitude of the tight bounds — culling still works, hit testing falls through to `onHitTest` for shapes where the hull is wildly off (a thin S-curve).

If a profile-driven need for tighter bounds materialises, Option 3 slots in as a successor without changing the public API — `recomputeBounds` is the only caller.

#### 1.4 — Acceptance Criteria

- A `<path d="M0 0 L100 100">` reports `bounds = { x: 0, y: 0, width: 100, height: 100 }` after `setProperty("d", …)`.
- The Phase 7 integration test for `onHitTest` rejection still passes (the override is consulted; the new bounds path is the *fallback*).
- A new test covers a curved path (`M0 0 C50 -50 100 50 150 0`) and asserts the control-point-hull bounds.
- The "always-paints regardless of viewport" test in `test/ui/canvas/culling.test.ts` for paths flips to assert culling now engages, with a comment explaining the v0.3.9 promotion.

### Phase 2: Group Bounds (Descendant Union)

#### 2.1 — The Deferral

`recomputeBounds` for `<group>` returns `zeroBounds()`, mirroring the path situation. The paint pass and hit-test walker recurse through groups regardless of viewport intersection (zero-area = always paint), then cull each child individually. v0.3.8 §4.4 specifies the eventual behaviour:

> For `group` elements the bounds are the union of all descendant bounds — computed lazily, cached, invalidated when any descendant geometry prop changes.

Currently nothing computes that union. The per-child intersect path is correct but pays `O(N_descendants)` rather than `O(1)` for any group whose subtree is entirely off-screen.

#### 2.2 — Motivations for Deferral

The interesting work isn't the union itself — it's *invalidation*. A correct lazy cache requires:

1. Every `setProperty` on a primitive that mutates a geometry key walks up its `parent` chain and marks each ancestor `<group>` dirty.
2. Every `insert` and `remove` invalidates the new and old parent `<group>`s up their respective chains.
3. The dirty bit clears on read of `el.bounds` (or whenever the group's bounds are recomputed).

This is a classic cache-invalidation problem and the test surface for it is wide: prop changes, list reorders (keyed `RefArray.map` reorders touch parent pointers), un-mounts, scope-driven cleanup. v0.3.8 already shipped two side maps for the implicit text wrapping (`textWrappers` / `wrapperToText`); adding a third state machine for group-bounds dirtiness — without first having a paint-pass *bottleneck* that justifies it — felt like premature optimisation. The fall-through to "recurse and child-cull" works correctly today.

#### 2.3 — Implementation Strategy Options

| Option | Approach | Approx. LOC | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | **Eager** — recompute the union in `setProperty` and `insert`/`remove`, walking the parent chain bottom-up. | ~30 | Simplest. Cost is paid every prop write; expensive for groups with thousands of descendants and frequent geometry mutations. |
| 2 | **Lazy with a dirty bit** (per `§4.4`) — `setProperty`/`insert`/`remove` mark the chain dirty; `el.bounds` is recomputed on the first read after a dirty mark and cached. | ~50 | Matches the spec. Amortised O(1) per write; cost paid once per frame on the read side (paint pass / hit test). |
| 3 | **Batched recomputation at flush boundary** — collect dirty groups during the rAF tick; recompute them once before paint reads the bounds. | ~40 | Marries to the existing rAF protocol; one well-defined recompute pass per frame. Slightly more orchestration. |
| 4 | **Skip the optimisation entirely** — leave child-by-child culling in place. | 0 | The status quo. `O(N)` intersect tests stays acceptable for the few-thousand-element scenes the diagramming target needs. |

**Recommendation: Option 2.** It matches the v0.3.8 spec and the "compute when read" pattern used elsewhere in aljabr (cf. `Derived` in `prelude/derived.ts`, where a dirty notification triggers eventual re-evaluation, not an immediate one). The dirty bit lives on the `CanvasElementNode` payload — no new variant, no new map.

If profiling shows that walking up the parent chain on every `setProperty` is itself the cost (deep trees, dense mutation), Option 3 becomes attractive — but only with that profile in hand.

#### 2.4 — Acceptance Criteria

- A `<group>` with a single far-off-screen child reports bounds equal to that child's bounds after the next read.
- Mutating a descendant primitive's `x` invalidates all ancestor groups' caches.
- Inserting / removing a child invalidates the immediate parent group and its ancestors.
- A new test in `test/ui/canvas/culling.test.ts` mounts a group with N children, places the entire group off-screen, and asserts that the paint pass emits zero `fillRect` calls (whereas the same scene under v0.3.8 emitted N-1 culled-child intersect tests).
- The reactive-list reorder test from `renderer.test.ts` keeps passing — the dirty walks must compose with `RefArray.map`'s keyed re-parenting.

### Phase 3: Text Bounds

#### 3.1 — The Deferral

`<text>` elements currently report `zeroBounds()`. The text layout pass (Phase 5) reads the *parent shape's* bounds when computing the wrapped text's `x`/`y`, so authored layouts work — but the text element itself contributes nothing to its own subtree's bounds. Hit testing on a label requires the click to land inside the parent shape's bounds; a label that overflows its parent (intentionally or by font fallback) is unhittable past the parent's edge.

#### 3.2 — Motivations for Deferral

Text bounds require font metrics. The only general-purpose source is `CanvasRenderingContext2D.measureText(content)`, which needs:

- A `ctx` reference (which `host.ts`'s `setProperty` doesn't have — it operates on the scene graph, not on a particular renderer).
- `ctx.font` set to the resolved font string before measuring (`fontWeight fontSize fontFamily`), which itself depends on `PaintContext` resolution. At `setProperty` time, the paint context isn't yet known — it's resolved during the paint walk.

The roadmap §5.2 spelled out *layout* (positioning text inside a parent's bounds) but did not require text *measurement* to ship in v0.3.8 — wrapping authoring against fixed shape parents avoids the question entirely. So text bounds were silently deferred along with path and group bounds.

#### 3.3 — Implementation Strategy Options

| Option | Approach | Approx. LOC | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | **Measure at paint time** — `paintShape` calls `ctx.measureText(content)` after composing `ctx.font`, writes the result into `el.bounds` for the next frame. | ~20 | Bounds are correct *one frame late* for the first paint and after every font/content change. Hit tests that fire before the first paint of a fresh element see `zeroBounds`. Simplest path; works in practice for interaction-driven UI (paint always happens before the user clicks). |
| 2 | **Shared offscreen canvas** — `host.ts` allocates a single `OffscreenCanvas` (or DOM `HTMLCanvasElement` fallback) and measures eagerly in `setProperty` whenever `content`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, or `fontWeight` changes. | ~40 | Bounds are always correct, even before the first paint. Resolves font through the same context resolution as paint, but at write time — needs to walk up to find the inherited values, which the paint pass also does. Best general behaviour; modest startup cost (offscreen canvas allocation, one per process). |
| 3 | **Heuristic estimate** — `width ≈ fontSize × 0.6 × content.length`, `height ≈ fontSize × 1.2`. | ~10 | No canvas needed, no measurement cost. Useful only for culling (overestimate is harmless); too imprecise for hit testing on proportional fonts. |
| 4 | **Defer to author** — expose `measureText(text, ctx)` as a utility, let the diagramming application opt into setting a `bounds` prop manually. | ~5 | Punts the problem. Encourages the same workaround we already have for paths via `onHitTest`. |

**Recommendation: Option 2 (shared offscreen canvas).** It matches the "eager on `setProperty`" pattern already used by every other primitive's bounds — there's no two-pass model elsewhere in the host, and introducing one for text alone (Option 1) creates a third state-machine class authors have to reason about. The offscreen canvas allocation is one-per-process; its cost is paid once.

The font-resolution piece — walking up to find the nearest `<group>` that overrides `fontFamily`/`fontSize`/`fontWeight` — already exists in `paint.ts`'s `deriveContext` walk; lifting the lookup into a shared helper is part of the work.

#### 3.4 — Acceptance Criteria

- A `<text content="Hello" fontSize=20>` with no explicit `x`/`y` reports `bounds.width > 0` and `bounds.height ≈ 20` after `setProperty("content", …)`.
- Changing `fontSize` re-measures and updates bounds.
- Changing `fontFamily` on an ancestor `<group>` triggers a re-measure on the descendant text (this requires the font-resolution helper to be re-runnable when ancestor context changes).
- A label that overflows its parent shape's right edge is hittable up to its actual rendered right edge.
- Existing text-layout tests continue to pass — the *positioning* logic doesn't change, only the *bounds* computation gains substance.

### 4.0 Out of Scope (Tracked)

These surfaced during v0.3.8 but are intentionally not part of v0.3.9. Each is recorded so a future version can lift it without re-discovering the context.

#### 4.1 — `CanvasNode` value-and-type re-export through the barrel

Today `aljabr/ui/canvas` exports the `CanvasNode` *type* but the *value* (the variant factory) lives only in `aljabr/ui/canvas/node`. This is forced by `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` rejecting a same-name `export { X }` + `export type { X }` pair through one barrel. v0.3.8 documented the workaround in `index.ts`. A future version could split `node.ts` into `node-types.ts` (types only) + `node-factory.ts` (value), letting both names re-export through the barrel without conflict — at the cost of an extra file. Defer until someone actually needs the factory through the public surface (the host's `createElement` / `createText` cover all known authoring sites).

#### 4.2 — `onHitTest` naming vs. the spec's original `hitTest`

v0.3.8 §6.4 was revised to use `onHitTest` because the reconciler's `on*` rule routes callback functions through without the reactive-getter trap. The spec's original `hitTest` name would require either (a) a special-case in the core renderer's reactive-prop check, or (b) a function-arity heuristic. Defer until either becomes warranted; the current naming is consistent with the rest of the event-handler family.

#### 4.3 — Word wrap for `<text>`

Explicitly out of scope per v0.3.8 §5.3. Authors integrate Pretext or similar; the renderer continues to single-line. Lifting this would require a layout engine, which v0.3.x does not have an appetite for.

#### 4.4 — `createPortal` for cross-renderer composition

Explicitly out of scope per v0.3.8 design constraints. Promotion to `aljabr/ui` waits on the diagramming-plugin author validating the userland pattern (mount a fresh renderer root, tie cleanup to the parent owner) in production. Once validated, a thin wrapper lands in core.

#### 4.5 — Per-frame matrix allocation in `hit-test.ts`

`hit-test.ts`'s `compose` allocates a fresh tuple per group on every hit walk. For scenes with deep group nesting and heavy pointer traffic this could show up in profiles. A pooled-matrix approach would amortise the cost; defer until a profile demands it.

### Design Constraints

- **Public API unchanged.** No new exports from `aljabr/ui/canvas/index.ts`. No new prop names. No new `JSX.IntrinsicElements` keys.
- **No new variants on `CanvasNode`.** Bounds-completeness fits inside the existing payload via `bounds` writes.
- **No regressions in v0.3.8 tests.** Every existing test file under `test/ui/canvas/` continues to pass without edits, except for the explicit "always paints regardless of viewport" assertions for path/group/text — those tests are flipped to assert the new culling behaviour, with a comment pointing at this roadmap.
- **No external dependencies introduced.** The path-string parser, group union walker, and offscreen-canvas measurement all use stdlib + browser APIs already in scope.

### Implementation Order

1. Phase 1: Path bounds (control-point hull parser).
2. Phase 2: Group bounds (lazy + dirty bit).
3. Phase 3: Text bounds (shared offscreen canvas).

Each phase ships with the test updates flagged in its acceptance criteria before the next begins. Phases 1 and 2 are independent and could ship in either order; Phase 3 depends only on the existing paint context resolution and is independent of the other two.

---

# v0.4.0.md

Source: https://github.com/jasuperior/aljabr/blob/main/docs/roadmap/v0.4.0.md

### **Aljabr Roadmap (v0.4.0): Prose Foundations**

**Strategic Vision**

The original motivation for aljabr was a text editor. v0.3.x built the foundations — algebraic data types, reactive primitives, a renderer abstraction with two production hosts (DOM and Canvas) — but the editor itself remained downstream of libraries that weren't quite right. The contenteditable surface in modern browsers is a chaotic event soup: input events fragment across `inputType` codes, composition events interleave with regular input during IME, paste lands raw HTML in the DOM before authors can intercept, and selection is owned by the browser's `Range` API which speaks DOM nodes and offsets — useless at the document-model level.

Existing solutions (ProseMirror, Lexical, Slate) all build *on top of* the DOM event soup and pay a recurring tax in hacking around it. v0.4.0 takes the opposite stance: **the renderer owns the DOM under contenteditable; the browser never writes to it.** Every browser intent flows through `beforeinput` (or composition handlers, or the paste interceptor), gets converted to a typed command, validates through a protocol that may reject it, and only then mutates the document model. The DOM is rewritten from the model — never read back to recover state.

This release lays the foundation. The renderer ships with a closed primitive set, a built-in command union, a default `apply` function, native browser selection, and read-only support. IME, paste, history, and keyboard bindings ship in v0.4.1; richer parsers and Schema-driven extensions ship in v0.4.2. Collaborative cursors and custom selection rendering are deferred to v0.5.0.

The package lives at `aljabr/ui/prose` — a sibling of `aljabr/ui/dom` and `aljabr/ui/canvas`. It ships its own JSX runtime at `aljabr/ui/prose/jsx-runtime` (third one alongside `dom/jsx-runtime` and `canvas/jsx-runtime`); authors point their TS config or per-file pragma at it for prose components. The author-facing surface returns `{ view, mount }` — the same shape `createRenderer` and `createCanvasRenderer` produce — but is constructed via `ProseRenderer.create(rootElement)`, mirroring the `Signal.create` / `Store.create` / `List.create` static-method convention. The author owns the document state as a `Dispatcher` (from v0.3.10's prelude additions) and binds it to the renderer via `<document state={doc}>` as a JSX prop. There is no separate controller object.

> **Footnote — renderer factory naming.** The existing `createRenderer` and `createCanvasRenderer` use the legacy `create*` free-function form. Going forward the convention is `<ReturnType>.create(...)` — a static method on a namespace named after the produced value. `ProseRenderer.create` adopts this immediately. A separate, non-blocking refactor pass (tracked for a future patch release) will migrate `createRenderer` → `Renderer.create` and `createCanvasRenderer` → `CanvasRenderer.create`. The shape of the returned `{ view, mount }` value stays the same in all three cases — only the call-site spelling changes.

### **Table of Contents**

- **1.0 Phase 1: Document Model**
    - _The closed primitive set, the marks model, and the JSX surface authors write against._
- **2.0 Phase 2: `EditorRange` and `RangePoint`**
    - _Tagged union for the cursor/selection/node-selection trichotomy; enriched coordinates carrying stable node IDs and logical line/column._
- **3.0 Phase 3: Built-in Command Union and Default `apply`**
    - _The command vocabulary, the protocol implementation that turns commands into document mutations, and the inverse-producing `apply` shape._
- **4.0 Phase 4: `ProseRenderer.create`**
    - _The renderer host, the `<document>` JSX element, and the `{ view, mount }` author surface._
- **5.0 Phase 5: Synthetic Events**
    - _The thin event surface (`onInput`, `onSelect`, `onFocus`, `onBlur`) exposed on `<document>`. (`onPaste` and `onCompose` ship in v0.4.1.)_
- **6.0 Phase 6: Native Selection Binding**
    - _Sync the `Dispatcher`'s cursor state into the browser `Selection`, and translate `selectionchange` into `SetCursor` commands._
- **7.0 Phase 7: `parse.jsx` and Read-Only Mode**
    - _The first parser — JSX → `DocumentState` — and the `readonly` prop that toggles editing without swapping components._
- **8.0 Out of Scope (Tracked)**
    - _Items deferred to v0.4.1, v0.4.2, v0.5.0, or beyond._

### Phase 1: Document Model

#### 1.1 — Primitive Set (Closed)

The renderer ships eight node types. Authors compose with these via JSX; custom semantic nodes (mentions, embeds, widgets) are *components* that render to these primitives, not new node types in the renderer.

```
Structural:  <document>, <break>
Block:       <block>, <heading level={1..6}>, <quote>, <code>
Inline:      <text>
Void:        <image>, <hr>
```

Notes on each:

- **`<document>`** is the root. Exactly one per `Dispatcher`. Carries the `state` prop (binding to a `Dispatcher`), the `bindings` prop (keyboard map; default in v0.4.1), and the `readonly` prop (Phase 7).
- **`<break>`** is a hard break inside a block (Shift-Enter behaviour). Distinct from a paragraph split.
- **`<block>`** is the default block — the "paragraph." Renamed from the working term `<paragraph>` because it is genuinely the default container, not a paragraph-specific primitive.
- **`<heading level>`** carries a `level` prop in `1..6`. Level is part of the payload, not the tag — there is one heading node, not six.
- **`<quote>`** is a blockquote container. Holds blocks (including nested quotes).
- **`<code>`** is a block-level code container. Renamed from the working term `<codeblock>` because there is no longer a competing inline `<code>` (inline code is the `code` mark on `<text>`). Carries an optional `language` prop.
- **`<text>`** is the only inline primitive. All inline formatting is expressed via marks on `<text>`. See Phase 1.2.
- **`<image>`** is a void node. Carries `src`, `alt`, and `caption` as props — captions do not have their own editable child element. Authors who need editable captions compose with a sibling `<text>` block.
- **`<hr>`** is a void horizontal rule.

**Why a closed set rather than an open node registry:** custom node behaviour (editability, void semantics, cursor containment) is expressible through props on existing primitives. A `<Mention>` JSX component renders to `<text editable={false} mention userId="123">@jamel</text>` — the renderer only needs to understand `<text>`. Opening the renderer to author-registered node types would add ceremony (NodeSpec interfaces, registration calls, lifecycle hooks) for capabilities that components already provide.

#### 1.2 — Marks Model

Inline formatting is **marks**, applied as props on `<text>`. Three categories:

- **Style marks (boolean):** `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `strike`, `code`. Each is a boolean prop.
- **Payload marks (object):** `link={{ href }}`, `color`, `backgroundColor`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`. Each is a typed prop carrying its data inline.
- **Custom marks (typed union):** `marks={[MarkSet.Mention({ userId: "..." }), MarkSet.Comment({ threadId: "..." })]}`. The `marks` prop accepts an array of `MarkSet` variants — one per author-defined mark on this `<text>` node. `MarkSet` is a union built with the same machinery as `ProseCommand`, so authors extend it via `MarkSet.merge({ Mention: (userId: string) => ({ userId }) })` and the schema layer serializes via `Schema.variant(MarkSet, {...})`.

Examples:

```tsx
<text bold>plain bold</text>
<text bold italic code>multiple style marks</text>
<text link={{ href: "https://..." }}>clickable</text>
<text color="#f00" backgroundColor="#ff0">highlighted</text>
<text bold marks={[MarkSet.Mention({ userId: "123" })]}>@jamel</text>
```

**Why a typed union and not a record:** custom marks need to be serializable through `aljabr/schema` for the internal-clipboard format and (eventually) collaborative-editing transports. A record-shaped `marks={{ mention: { userId } }}` prop has no place to declare per-key payload schemas; a `MarkSet` union does (it composes with `Schema.variant` directly). It also opens marks to `match()` exhaustiveness checking for authors who pattern over them in their own components. The cost is one extra wrapping (`MarkSet.Mention(payload)` instead of `{ mention: payload }`) — accepted as the price of typed extensibility.

**DOM mapping (default):**

- Style marks emit minimal HTML: `bold` → `<strong>`, `italic` → `<em>`, `underline` → CSS, `strike` → `<s>`, `code` → `<code>`.
- Payload marks emit attributes or wrapping elements: `link` → `<a href>`, `color` → inline `style="color:..."`, font marks → inline styles.
- Custom marks default to `data-*` attributes derived from their tag (`MarkSet.Mention({ userId: "123" })` → `data-mention-user-id="123"`).

Authors can override default rendering for custom marks by providing a per-variant `render` function — that's a v0.4.2 ergonomic; v0.4.0 ships only the default mapping.

#### 1.3 — Implementation Strategy

Document nodes are a recursive tagged union. Because TypeScript can't infer the recursive `ProseNode[]` field while inferring the union itself, we follow the same pattern `Validation` uses in the codebase: declare each variant's `Variant<>` type alias first, then build the union via `union(...).typed({...})` with explicit casts.

```ts
import { union, type Variant } from "aljabr"

export type Document  = Variant<"Document",  { children: ProseNode[] }>
export type Block     = Variant<"Block",     { children: ProseNode[] }>
export type Heading   = Variant<"Heading",   { level: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6; children: ProseNode[] }>
export type Quote     = Variant<"Quote",     { children: ProseNode[] }>
export type Code      = Variant<"Code",      { language: string | null; children: ProseNode[] }>
export type Text      = Variant<"Text",      { content: string; marks: MarkSet[] }>
export type Image     = Variant<"Image",     { src: string; alt: string | null; caption: string | null }>
export type HardBreak = Variant<"HardBreak", {}>
export type Hr        = Variant<"Hr",        {}>

export type ProseNode =
    | Document | Block | Heading | Quote | Code
    | Text | Image | HardBreak | Hr

export const ProseNode = union({}).typed({
    Document:  (children: ProseNode[]) => ({ children }) as Document,
    Block:     (children: ProseNode[]) => ({ children }) as Block,
    Heading:   (level: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6, children: ProseNode[]) => ({ level, children }) as Heading,
    Quote:     (children: ProseNode[]) => ({ children }) as Quote,
    Code:      (language: string | null, children: ProseNode[]) => ({ language, children }) as Code,
    Text:      (content: string, marks: MarkSet[]) => ({ content, marks }) as Text,
    Image:     (src: string, alt: string | null, caption: string | null) => ({ src, alt, caption }) as Image,
    HardBreak: () => ({}) as HardBreak,
    Hr:        () => ({}) as Hr,
})
```

Each variant carries a stable node ID assigned at construction (or read from a JSX `id` prop if present). IDs are non-enumerable on the variant payload to avoid serialization noise; they are read via a `getNodeId(node)` helper.

#### 1.4 — Acceptance Criteria

- All eight primitives are exported from `aljabr/ui/prose`.
- JSX type definitions exist for each primitive, with prop types matching the union variant payloads.
- A new test file `test/ui/prose/document-model.test.ts` covers: variant construction, node ID assignment and stability, custom-mark composition (`MarkSet.merge` adds new variants without touching the built-in style/payload props), block-vs-inline placement constraints (the renderer rejects `<text>` directly under `<document>` without a containing block).
- Documentation in `docs/api/prose/document-model.md` describes each primitive, the marks model, and the closed-set rationale.

### Phase 2: `EditorRange` and `RangePoint`

#### 2.1 — Shape
